REVELATIONS AFTER A SECRET LAWSUIT.

label: text
text: Berlin, July 25.—The revelation that General Ludendorff, the German National leader, attempted to send his personal fortune out of the country in 1922, when the export of capital was forbidden, followed an action which he brought against Herr Adolf Borchardt; his banker.

label: text
text: It appears that the general eager to save the small fortune which accrued from his post-war literary activities, instructed his banker to remit his money abroad, and to purchase for him gilded foreign securities.

label: text
text: The general's plan was detected after one or two remittances were made to a Swiss bank, which subsequently went bankrupt, and his fortune disappeared during the inflation.

label: text
text: "General Ludendorff sued" the banker for "the money which had thus been lost," and although the trial was held in camera the affair leaked out. "The former military idol of Germany is said to have now no other means than his pension.

label: paragraph_title
text: SCAVENGERS' STRIKE

label: text
text: CITY IN A DEPLORABLE CONDITION.

label: text
text: Bombay, August 27.

label: text
text: Following the unrest among the street scavengers owing to the Municipality's proposal to reduce the pay of new employees by Rs. 5 monthly the majority of the scavengers have struck and the streets of a large part of the city are unswept though the cut does not apply to old employees.

label: text
text: It is stated that legal action against the strikers has been launched. Bailable warrants have been issued against 40' strikers chosen from all the wards of the city.

label: paragraph_title
text: Bombay, August 28."

label: text
text: The sweepers and scavengers, who for two days past have held the city at the point of the broom, and who are demanding the restoration of the five-rupee cut in wages of newly-appointed hands, have been thwarted by the Corporation.

label: text
text: Twenty-one men were arrested and brought before the Magistrate to-day. Two were convicted and sentenced to two months' hard labour on a charge of striking without two months' notice as required by the Bombay Municipal Employees' Act.

label: text
text: Subsequently the men, as a result of consultations, agreed to resume to-morrow, upon which decision further hearing was postponed.

label: text
text:
The accumulations of refuse in many parts of the city have been tackled by substitute sweepers from neighbouring parts.
Announcement was made yesterday by Mr. Yasuji Shimizu, general manager of the Ntppon Yusen Kaishn, of the reaching of a decision by the corporation to erect a new office building in Shanghai.
In an interview with the “Japan Times,” Mr. Shimizu explained that the new structure would be built on the site of the old Yokohama Special Bank on the Whampoo waterfront, overlooking the public gardens close to the British Consulate. The purchase of the Yokohama Special Bank building and premises of 600 tsubo of land was approved at a director's meeting recently, Mr. Shimizu said.

label: text
text:
To Cost Million Yen.
Decision to erect a new building at an expenditure of a million yen was made because of the faith held by officials of the Japanese shipping concern in the future of Shanghai according to Mr. Shimizu.

label: text
text: Local businessmen have long foreseen the further expansion of the Chinese port city and to meet the growing passenger trade which was accelerated with the acquisition of the Toyo Kisen Kaisha fleet, directors of the establishment unanimously agreed on the necessity of opening new and larger quarters in Shanghai, the general manager of the Nippon Yusen Kaisha explained.

label: text
text: The old Yokohama Specie Bank building will be temporarily renovated at a cost of Tls. 40,000 to house the booking office now quartered at the Palace Hotel. The general office is located at Hongkew.

label: text
text: The proposed new building is in the very heart of Shanghai's business and marine quarters; and within easy reach of the foreign and Chinese business centres. The old office of the Nippon Xusen Kaisha were located near the Japanese Consulate. The former building was erected more than 10 years ago. It will be pulled down in the near future and a modern warehouse built on the site.

label: text
text: Parliament has been discussing the purchase of Bute House in South Audley Street, London, as an official residence for Egyptian Ministers.

label: text
text:

The resolution expressed the desirability of re-converting Bute House in order to accommodate the Minister and his officers and the Consulate Educational Mission. Times of Ceylon.
STRONG DECLARATION IN HIS WILL.

label: paragraph_title
text: VON BISSING'S BAN.

label: text
text: The will of Baron Walter Adolphus von Bissing, half-brother of the German Military Governor of Belgium, which was published recently, is notable for its strong anti-German feeling.

label: text
text: ENGLISH ESTATE

label: text
text:
Baron von Bissing, a German by birth and a naturalised British subject, died domiciled in Italy, aged 70. Formerly he was for many years a prominent resident of Hove.
He left, exclusive of settled and foreign estate, unsettled property in England valued at £1,178, with net personality £1,136. Probate of the will, dated last April, has been granted to his widow, Baroness von Bissing, of 50. Tedworth Square, Chelsea, S.W. The Baron stated in his will:—

label: text
text:
“I desire particularly to express in the most emphatic and precise terms that under no circumstances whatever is any German, whether relation of mine or otherwise,” to have any voice or right in or over the guardianship or upbringing of “my children.”
He left: £500 to his solicitor, Edward A. L. Smith, Gray's Inn Square, W.C., in appreciation of his services, and all his other property to his widow.

label: text
text: A well-known Bishop tells a story of a visit to a small town where he was awakened one morning by a clear soprano voice singing a famous hymn. He could not help meditating on the piety of his hostess. Speaking to her at breakfast of the pleasure it had given him he received the unexpected answer, "Good gracious! That's the hymn I boil the eggs by three verses for soft and five for hard."

label: text
text: Every year the flor-1 committee of the C.P.R. has the stupendous task of supplying the seeds, trees, shrubs and plants to thousands of stations from Saint John to Victoria. Bulbs are supplied and planted in the fall, rearing their faunty heads with the melting of the snows in the spring.

label: text
text: The seeds are propagated under glass by experienced gardeners with a view to being transplanted when raised. In addition the committee sends out many thousands of seed packets to station agents and also for use in section formen's gardens, bunk houses and around shops. Enormous quintiles of bedding stock are also provided and among these are geraniums, cannas, asters, panales, salvin, petunias.

label: text
text:
Upper-Kenoga Station Garden. Lower left-Looking down on artistic Port McNicoll Station Garden. Lower right—"Countess of Dufferin", first C.P.R. engine to enter Winnipeg in her summer finery.
Living up to its title as the "Garden Railway", thousands of trees, shrubs and perenials were shipped out over the whole Canadian Pacific Railway system early in May this year. These included willows, poplars, lilac, spires, honeysuckle, syringa, weiglia, carragana, hydrangea, and many others. The perenials include roses of the climber and rambling variety and of all shades of color, tiger lilies, Iceland poppies, aquilegia, dianthus, Sweet William, pyrethrum, delphineum.
marigolds, stirrhinum phiox kochias, zinnlas, venbenas and alyssum.

label: text
text:
the Canadian Pacific Railway about thirty-five years ago. The majority of the gardens are laid out and looked after by employees of the system. Locomotive firemen, signal towermen, watchmen, bunkhouse attendants and others take a great interest in the gardens with the help of horticulturists. Every employee is alive to the importance and the pleasure of making the railway stations blossom. Each one of them is filled with a healthy sense of emulation and the desire to make his own garden the beauty spot of the railway. The men treat the whole plan as a hobby. All make the supreme yearly effort to win the general manager's cup, a worthy trophy emblematic of the best floral display along C.P.R. tracks. But the prices are not limited to this. Every general superintendent offers a prize for his own district each superintendent gives one for his division and every roadmaster offers one for his sub-division. During the Great War about 2,000 gardens were converted into vegetable-raising grounds and produced large quantities of food supplies for the men.
